title: Reykjavík’s 1986 summit ended with no deal, but led to a ban on a whole class of missiles
body: On 10 October 2026 Reykjavík [opened Höfði house](https://reykjavik.is/en/news/2026/open-house-hofdi-40th-anniversary-summit) to mark 40 years since US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met there, on 11 and 12 October 1986. They discussed getting rid of all ballistic missiles, and even all nuclear weapons, within ten years, but the talks broke down over Reagan’s Strategic Defense Initiative, a missile-defence research programme that Gorbachev wanted kept in the laboratory. One idea survived: no intermediate-range missiles in Europe. On 8 December 1987 the two leaders signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, which banned every ground-launched missile with a range of 500 to 5,500 km. By the deadline of 1 June 1991, [2,692 had been destroyed](https://www.armscontrol.org/factsheets/intermediate-range-nuclear-forces-inf-treaty-glance), 846 American and 1,846 Soviet, and each side’s inspectors checked the other’s sites. The United States withdrew in 2019, saying Russia had broken the treaty with a new missile, which Russia denied.

slides.question: The summit led to a 1987 treaty banning a class of missiles. How many did the US and Soviet Union destroy by June 1991?
slides.explanation: 2,692: 846 by the United States and 1,846 by the Soviet Union, every ground-launched missile with a range of 500 to 5,500 km.

slides.alt: Animation on old file paper: the white Höfði house in Reykjavík, cards for Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, a memo stamped no agreement, two zeros for missiles in Europe, the 1987 treaty, a range ruler with the banned 500 to 5,500 km band, missile marks crossed off and a timeline to 2019.

slides.prompt: Choose how a missile is launched and how far it can fly. Find an intermediate-range missile that the INF Treaty still allowed.
slides.takeaway: The treaty banned only missiles launched from the ground with ranges of 500 to 5,500 km. The same range fired from a ship or a plane was not covered, nor were shorter or longer ranges.

slides.heading: From Höfði to the end of the treaty

events.text: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev meet at Höfði: no deal
They sign the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty
The US withdraws; the treaty ends

left.label: Banned
left.text: US and Soviet missiles launched from the ground, with ranges of 500 to 5,500 km.

right.label: Not covered
right.text: Missiles fired from ships or planes, and missiles with shorter or longer ranges.

slides.question: Why did the Reykjavík summit of October 1986 end without an agreement?
options: Iceland refused to host a signing
slides.explanation: Mikhail Gorbachev wanted the US Strategic Defense Initiative, research on missile defence, kept to laboratories for ten years. Ronald Reagan refused.

source.label: Arms Control Association: The INF Treaty at a Glance
